title: Large Language Models and You
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) explain large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Llama: neural networks trained on massive text that predict likely next words using embeddings and transformers. They cover GPT-4's gains over GPT-3.5 on tests, prompting to improve math, hallucinations (fake legal cases, the elephant-egg error, a fabricated science formula, the eating disorder helpline incident), image-input capabilities, the DALL-E and Getty Images copyright dispute, corporate data privacy concerns, job displacement of white-collar workers, productivity and GDP projections, IBM's hiring pause, the Hollywood writers' strike and AI concerns, and the singularity. The episode closes with a listener mail story about a conception-related podcast listen and sign-off.

entities.name: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: The hosts joke about whether the episode is really them or AI-generated, and tease the topic of large language models.

segments.title: What large language models are
segments.summary: Josh defines large language models as AI algorithms trained on huge amounts of English text that recognize patterns and simulate conversation. They discuss the End of the World series episode on AI and how the field has moved quickly since 2018.
topics: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Brain analogy and autocomplete
segments.summary: The hosts compare neural networks to the human brain and explain that LLMs work like autocomplete, predicting likely next words based on probability.

segments.title: Connections and weights in word prediction
segments.summary: Josh explains how word inputs and outputs form huge numbers of connections, with weights emphasizing some associations (such as John Coltrane and A Love Supreme) over others.

segments.title: Word clustering, embeddings, and lack of understanding
segments.summary: Words cluster by how often they appear together, which the models use to create meaning numerically via embeddings. Josh stresses that LLMs do not understand meaning, and that this underlies hallucinations.

segments.title: Self-learning, human feedback, and the transformer
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how models learn on their own and improve via reinforcement learning from human feedback. Josh covers the 2017 Google transformer paper, which lets models analyze all text at once, and the black-box problem. Iheart Intro notes the GPT name meaning generative pre-trained transformer.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Rapid timeline and specialized models
segments.summary: They trace the rapid timeline from ChatGPT's November 2022 launch to GPT-4 in March 2023, and note companies building specialized models by adding software or training on domain data.

segments.title: Multimodal image input and arms race
segments.summary: Josh describes GPT-4 accepting images, with a demo of a sketched website turned into working code. He argues the race among private companies makes slowing AI unlikely.

segments.title: Test scores and math performance
segments.summary: The hosts cite GPT-4's bar exam and AP exam results, improving from GPT-3.5, and note weaker math performance that prompting and add-on tools aim to fix.

segments.title: Hallucinations explained
segments.summary: The hosts define hallucinations as confident but false outputs and give the example of the model claiming elephants lay the largest mammal eggs. Josh explains the model lacks fact-checking and truth concepts.

segments.title: Real-world AI errors
segments.summary: Examples include a lawyer who submitted fake case citations generated by ChatGPT, a Meta science model that invented formulas, and an AI-written article on compound interest with errors and plagiarism.

segments.title: Eating disorder helpline chatbot
segments.summary: The National Eating Disorder Association replaced its human hotline with a chatbot that gave weight-loss advice to people with eating disorders, and it was taken offline. The hosts note newer models score better on accuracy.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before discussing economics and jobs.

segments.title: Jobs at risk from AI
segments.summary: Josh notes that unlike earlier automation that hit manual labor, LLMs threaten white-collar knowledge jobs and artists. The hosts joke about farmers being safe.

segments.title: AI art, copyright, and corporate data concerns
segments.summary: The hosts discuss DALL-E image generation and Getty Images suing for infringement, arguing mashups do not count as transformative use. They also discuss companies restricting employee chatbot use over data exposure and Meta's Llama and Alpaca models.

segments.title: Workplace AI use and productivity
segments.summary: Examples include real estate listings and medical symptom lists. A Fishbowl survey found 40 percent of working professionals use AI tools at work, and nearly 70 percent of them hide it from bosses.

segments.title: Productivity, GDP, and the economic outlook
segments.summary: Goldman Sachs estimated about a 7 percent GDP increase over ten years from productivity gains. The hosts doubt displaced workers will find new jobs and debate universal basic income versus widening wealth gaps. They note middle management may be most at risk.

segments.title: Historical technology and the Hollywood writers' strike
segments.summary: The hosts note technology's mixed history and discuss the WGA strike, where writers oppose AI replacement and studios proposed assessing AI on a year-to-year basis. They worry about AI-generated clickbait and scripts.

segments.title: Human-created content and digital likeness
segments.summary: Josh predicts demand for human-written work and notes that AI-written web content may later train other models. Iheart Intro cites Justine Bateman on actors scanned for digital likenesses used in perpetuity, and IBM's CEO Arvind Krishna saying 30 percent of back-office jobs could be replaced; IBM paused hiring for about 8,000 roles, and Dropbox announced layoffs citing AI.

segments.title: Coding AI and the singularity
segments.summary: The hosts discuss AI writing code so that it could create new AI models, and define the singularity as when AI understands itself. They say the outcome is unknown and express unease.

segments.title: Listener mail: Conception
segments.summary: A listener reports that his wife and he conceived a child while playing the episode How Coal Works in the background, and that they named their son Cole. Josh and Chuck read the email and invite listeners to write in.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Iheart Intro reminds listeners that Stuff You Should Know is a production of iHeartRadio and gives the email address.
